In brief

Parody. "A most interesting discussion took place in the ancient hall of Brian O'ciarnain's in Sraid na Bretaine Bheag, under the auspices of Sluagh na h-Eireann [...] The laity included P. Fay, T. Quirke, etc., etc.": the orotund newspaper-style writing of the execution and talking dog parodies returns in this passage responding to the Citizen's advocacy of native Irish sports. Sloppy bar talk becomes the learned discourse of debating societies, scattered barhounds become the gathered ranks of important social professions, the belting of a popular anthem becomes an operatic tour de force, and sporting matches become the pastimes of mythic heroes. For the first time in Cyclops but not the last, the Catholic church supplies matter of cyclopean superabundance.

At more length

Joe Hynes has been praising the Citizen not only as a great former athlete but also as the man "that made the Gaelic sports revival." In a single sentence the narrator recounts their talking "about Irish sports and shoneen games [...] and building up a nation once again." Then he notes Bloom's ridiculous objection that violent exercise can be bad for people with weak hearts.

In response to this briefly summarized exchange, the parody offers a fulsome account of what was said "in the ancient hall of Brian O'ciarnain's" (Barney Kiernan's) "in Sraid na Bretaine Bheag" (Little Britain Street) "under the auspices of Sluagh na h-Eireann" (the Host of Ireland, a patriotic sports group mentioned earlier in connection with Nannetti's parliamentary junket). The Irish names locate this discussion solidly in the Revivalist context of the Gaelic League and the Gaelic Athletic Assocation, and the topic under discussion is "the revival of ancient Gaelic sports and the importance of physical culture, as understood in ancient Greece and ancient Rome and ancient Ireland, for the development of the race."

As founder of the GAA, the Citizen is "The venerable president of the noble order." He chairs the meeting and delivers a "magnificent oration" on "the revivability of the ancient games and sports of our ancient panceltic forefathers." Joe Hynes seconds his views, adding the mythological endorsement that these games were "practised morning and evening by Finn MacCool." Bloom voices "the negative" viewpoint and encounters "a mixed reception of applause and hisses." The chairman ends all discussion of the matter by belting out a rousing rendition of A Nation Once Again, a performance that rivals Caruso and Garibaldi. The audience erupts in applause, and "The proceedings then terminated."

This cyclopean exaggeration of a trivial conversational exchange feels rather tame and derivative after some of the brilliant eruptions that have preceded it. Its strangest feature, by far, is the long list of clergymen that concludes it. Joe Hynes is a newspaper reporter and J. J. O'Molloy a lawyer, so it makes some sense that the parody would note the presence of "representatives of the press and the bar and the other learned professions." But no priests are drinking in Barney Kiernan's, so the listing of "many prominent members of the clergy" seems a particularly fantastic invention. Later in Cyclops a long catalogue of saints and other religious men and women will be prompted by Martin Cunningham saying, "God bless all here is my prayer," but God and the church have not come up in the discussion of Irish sports.

Nor does there seem to be more than a germ of truth in calling the clergymen "prominent." The first man named in the list, William Delany, was the president of Joyce's university, UCD, from 1883 to 1909. The second, Gerald Molloy, was rector of the Catholic University of Ireland in Dublin at the same time. And the third, Patrick Kavanagh, had published a well-known history of the Rebellion of 1798 in 1874. After these three academic notables, however, the other twenty-one clergymen are run-of-the-mill parish priests, curates-in-charge (apprentice priests), vicars (minor bureaucrats), provincials (leaders of priestly communities), and friars, their names scooped up from the Thom's directory. The impression they make in the reporting of the meeting depends chiefly on their sheer number.

Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner offer a convincing contextual explanation for the swarm of priests, quoting from Timothy McMahon's Grand Opportunity: The Gaelic Revival and Irish Society, 1893-1910 (2008): "there is considerable evidence to support the perception that the Catholic church dominated the language movement: members of the Catholic hierarchy spoke frequently and favourably at Gaelic League functions; revivalists paid very close attention to the minutest signs of clerical support for their cause; and many Catholic priests and nuns were prominent in the League, particularly at the branch level" (34). It would seem, then, that in this cyclopean parody Joyce faithfully reflected what he knew of meetings of groups like the Gaelic League and the Gaelic Athletic Association. Their eagerness to win the endorsement of Catholic clergy members probably did not endear them to him.

John Hunt 2026
